h1: The 6 Best Kindle Alternatives of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: six e-readers that beat the Kindle on library borrowing, file formats, color screens or Android freedom, sorted by use.
summary: The Kobo Libra Colour is our top Kindle alternative for library borrowers who want buttons and a color screen. The PocketBook Verse Pro is the pick for people with big collections of EPUB and other files, and the PocketBook InkPad Color 3 has the largest color display. The OBOOK6 is the budget route to a real Android reader.
intro: The usual mistake when leaving the Kindle is shopping for a better screen and forgetting that the real lock-in is your book library. Before buying anything, find out where your books live: Amazon purchases, a public library app, or a folder of files on your computer. Each answer points at a different reader.

We ranked six alternatives on paper using the spec sheets and owner reports. Library support, file formats, page-turn buttons, screen type and price bracket carried the most weight. Prices appear as buckets because they change often.

products.name: Kobo Libra Colour, 7" Glare-Free Colour E Ink Kaleido 3, Waterproof, Black
products.verdict: The closest thing to a better Kindle for people who borrow library books.
products.description:
The Libra Colour pairs a 7-inch Kaleido 3 color E Ink screen with physical page-turn buttons and built-in OverDrive and Libby support. It is waterproof, and it costs $200-500.

The top spot goes to it as the only pick here that combines library borrowing, buttons, and color in one body. The InkPad Color 3 below has a bigger screen but lacks the page buttons and library focus.

Best for readers who borrow from a public library and like a one-handed grip. The caveat is the price bracket, which is the highest in this ranking.
cons: Color panel less crisp than black and white
products.idealFor: Library borrowers who want buttons and color.
products.skipIf: You buy mostly from Amazon and want its store.

products.name: PocketBook Verse Pro E-Reader Waterproof, 6" E-Ink Carta HD, Azure
products.verdict: Opens nearly any file you already own, with no conversion.
products.description:
The Verse Pro has a 6-inch E Ink Carta HD display, waterproofing, text-to-speech, and both Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. Its standout is broad format support, and it costs $100-200.

Second place fits because file freedom is what most people leaving Kindle actually miss, and this one delivers it at a mid price. It loses to the Kobo since there is no integrated library borrowing listed.

Buy it if you keep books as files on a computer. Expect a small, black-and-white screen.
products.idealFor: Readers with a large folder of non-Kindle files.
products.skipIf: You want color or a larger page.

products.name: PocketBook InkPad Color 3, 7.8" Color E-Paper Display, Waterproof
products.verdict: The roomiest color page among the closed-system readers.
products.description:
The InkPad Color 3 has a 7.8-inch color E-paper display, a built-in speaker, 32GB of storage, and a waterproof body, at $200-500.

Third place reflects that the larger page suits comics, textbooks, and PDFs, yet it costs about as much as the Kobo while skipping the library integration and buttons.

Choose it for graphic content or documents. The cost is a heavier, bulkier device than the 6-inch models.

products.name: PocketBook Verse Pro Color, 6" E Ink Kaleido 3, IPX8 Waterproof
products.verdict: Color without the Android fiddling, at a mid price.
products.description:
This is a 6-inch Kaleido 3 color E Ink reader with an IPX8 waterproof rating and a closed, simple software system, for $100-200.

It lands below the black-and-white Verse Pro since color panels trade sharpness for hue, but it undercuts the InkPad Color 3 and Libra Colour on price.

Pick it for color covers and magazines on a small device. Skip it if your priority is the sharpest text.
products.idealFor: Readers who want cheap color in a small body.
products.skipIf: You need the crispest black text.

products.name: PocketBook Verse E-Reader, 6" E-Ink Carta HD, Bright Blue
products.verdict: File freedom and a memory card slot for the least money in the Pocketbook line.
products.description:
The standard Verse has a 6-inch Carta HD screen, broad format support, a memory card slot, and up to a month of battery per the listing, at $100-200.

Fifth place comes from how it gives up the waterproofing and extras of the Verse Pro. In return, the card slot lets you expand storage cheaply.

A sensible buy for readers who want formats and a long battery without paying extra. Do not expect waterproofing from the spec list.
products.idealFor: Budget readers with files to open.

products.name: OBOOK6 eReader (32GB), 6" 300ppi Glare-Free Display, Android
products.verdict: The cheapest way to put real Android apps on an E Ink screen.
products.description:
The OBOOK6 runs genuine Android on a 6-inch 300ppi glare-free display with 32GB of storage for $50-100, the lowest here.

Last place follows because open Android on a low-cost device is a project, not an appliance, and it comes from a lesser-known brand than Kobo or PocketBook. The upside is you can install the reading apps you already use, including Kindle.

Good for tinkerers on a tight budget. Expect more setup and fewer polish touches.
products.idealFor: Budget readers who want their own apps.
products.skipIf: You want a polished plug-and-play device.

whatMatters.detail: OverDrive and Libby let you borrow ebooks free from a public library. Some readers include it and others need sideloading. Look for the named apps in the product bullets.
Kindle devices are fussy about formats other than Amazon's. Readers with broad support open EPUB and similar files directly. Check the format list on the listing.
Color E Ink adds hue but slightly dulls the contrast and sharpness of text. It helps for comics and covers. Look for Kaleido in the title and expect softer text.
Buttons let you flip pages without touching the screen, useful one-handed or with gloves. Touch-only readers can feel clumsy. The listing will mention physical buttons if present.
Android lets you install any reading app but requires setup and drains battery faster. A closed system works at once. Check whether the listing says Android.

howToChoose.intro: Your existing library is the strongest guide.

cards.label: Color
cards.text: Good for covers, comics and charts but softer for text. The Kobo Libra Colour, InkPad Color 3 and Verse Pro Color use it.

cards.label: Black and white
cards.text: Sharper and cheaper for novels. The PocketBook Verse Pro, Verse and OBOOK6 use it.

howToChoose.note: Most novel readers should default to black and white.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Named OverDrive or Libby support in the listing bullets.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Kobo Libra Colour lists built-in OverDrive and Libby, making it the straightforward choice.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want library borrowing, buttons and color together; the Kobo Libra Colour delivers all three.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You read plain text novels; the PocketBook Verse or OBOOK6 is enough.

faq.a: Not natively on Kobo or PocketBook. The Android-based OBOOK6 can run the Kindle app.

faq.q: Which one works with my public library?
faq.a: The Kobo Libra Colour lists built-in OverDrive and Libby support.

faq.q: Is color E Ink worth it over black and white?
faq.a: Only for comics and illustrated books. Text looks softer, so novel readers should skip it.

faq.q: Do I need to convert my files?
faq.a: The PocketBook Verse line lists broad format support, so most files open directly.
The Kobo Libra Colour, Verse Pro, Verse Pro Color and InkPad Color 3 are listed as waterproof.

faq.q: Is the OBOOK6 a good idea?
faq.a: It is a budget Android device with a lesser-known brand. It suits people who like tinkering.

finalTake: The Kobo Libra Colour is the best all-round replacement if you borrow library books. The PocketBook Verse Pro wins for people with files, and the InkPad Color 3 for big pages. The OBOOK6 is the budget gamble.
